title: The Maharaja close
hookLine: forty years of a Punjab kingdom, from Lahore's open gate to the samadhi

cards: Lay two pictures side by side. In the first, a young chief with one eye rides through a gate of Lahore that someone inside has opened for him.
In the second, a pale building with a gilded dome stands by the same city's Fort, holding his ashes. Everything in this part of the path happened between those two pictures.
Histories count about forty years from the day he took Lahore to the day he died.

teach.h: THE RISE: FROM A MISL TO LAHORE.
teach.b: A boy born in Gujranwala, scarred by smallpox and blind in one eye, led his misl young, with help around him. Lahore opened its gate to him.
He took the title of Maharaja, but ruled as the Sarkar-e-Khalsa, the government in the Khalsa's name.

Look at what he built: gold on the Harmandir, a river line on the Sutlej he chose to keep, an army drilled in new ways by officers from many lands, Hari Singh Nalwa on the frontier, Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar joining the kingdom, the Koh-i-Noor on his arm, a court of many faiths, painters at work, gifts to Patna and Nanded, and a reputation for rarely ordering death.
And Maharani Jind Kaur, the youngest queen, whose hardest days are still ahead.
Then what he couldn't hold. He bowed at the Akal Takht and accepted its rebuke, so even he answered to something above the throne. But he left no settled way to hand on what he'd built.

After he died, the kingdom came apart in the hands of rivals: two heirs lost, Sher Singh killed, a child on the throne, the army louder than the court. A kingdom so much one man's work was fragile without him.
Forty years is a single working life: long enough to change the map, short enough that people who saw it begin could see it end. That's the sorrow in this story, and the honesty too.
Some things are great and brief at once.
Tomorrow a new part of the path begins, and it's harder: war with the British.

how: Sikhs remember Maharaja Ranjit Singh's reign as the time of a Sikh kingdom in the Punjab, and tell its story from his taking of Lahore to his death, and the troubles that followed.

practice: Bring to mind something good in your life that didn't last as long as you wanted: a friendship, a home, a season, a person.
Picture its beginning, then what it built in you, then the end, without rushing past it, and notice what's still with you from it, even now. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
